description: We are six high school students from South Korea passionate about astronomy and space science. We're interested in lunar exploration, data analysis, and applying AI to real NASA data. This is our first Space Apps Challenge, and our goal is to learn, collaborate, and build a meaningful project. Our team is full, but we're always happy to connect with other participants and mentors!
summary: Flame Finder helps habitat designers and students see which of NASA's microgravity combustion experiments apply to the air planned for Moon and Mars bases (8.2 psia, about 34% oxygen). It ranks all 24 combustion investigations in NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) for any oxygen level and pressure, using 876 test-level rows from the PSI experimental tables. It shows where the evidence is thin: only 19 recorded ISS tests were run near Moon and Mars base air, and none at lunar or Martian gravity. In the closest tests, droplet flames went out on their own 0 of 17 times, compared with 14 of 29 in cabin air. A question box answers from the tables with numbered dataset sources, in English or Korean.
details:
What it does. You choose an atmosphere (ISS cabin, Shuttle pre-spacewalk, or the planned Moon and Mars base air) or set oxygen and pressure. Flame Finder scores each PSI combustion investigation out of 100 with a visible breakdown: recorded tests near the selection (40), oxygen match (20), pressure match (15), fire-safety relevance (15) and open test data (10). Missing values score zero. Each experiment page shows its tested conditions, a plot of its tests against your selection, and a dataset citation with its DOI.

How it works. We read the PSI investigation records and downloaded the experimental tables for all 24 investigations. From five tables (PSI-10, PSI-25, PSI-39, PSI-69, PSI-159) we extracted oxygen and pressure for 876 individual ISS tests, and from FLEX (PSI-69) the outcome and burning rate of 274 droplet tests. The site is a single static page with the data built in, served by GitHub Pages. Code: https://github.com/Sibisy/flame-finder

Ask the data. On the live GitHub Pages site, a keyword planner turns a question into a small JSON query; when the site is deployed with its Netlify function, a language model (Claude Haiku 4.5 through Netlify AI Gateway) does this instead. The page runs the query on the tables and computes the numbers. With the model available, it then writes a 2–4 sentence explanation with numbered sources, and the browser checks every number in it against the computed result; if one does not match, it shows a computed summary instead. Six example questions work without AI.

Benefits and impact. NASA plans higher-oxygen, lower-pressure air for surface habitats so crews can start spacewalks sooner, and fire spreads more easily in that air. Flame Finder makes it quick to see which measurements apply and where new tests are needed, with every number traceable to NASA's open data. The Korean interface opens the data to students in Korea.

Tools. HTML, CSS and JavaScript; Python for data extraction; GitHub and GitHub Pages; Netlify Functions and AI Gateway (optional server for the language model); the Paperlogy typeface.

Design. Our team's own presentation deck (one idea per screen, Morph transitions, palette and type), Apple product pages (scroll-linked transitions), NASA Earthdata Search (filters, results, details), NASA Worldview (data availability bars), ClinicalTrials.gov (filter counts), Semantic Scholar (term definitions) and Perplexity (numbered sources). Photos: NASA.

Use of AI. In development, AI assistants helped write parts of the code, the English and Korean text, and the data-extraction scripts; we reviewed the results and checked numbers against the source tables. In the product, the optional language model only plans queries and words explanations; it never produces the numbers. No AI-generated images, video or audio are used.
